rv.q: When focused on the crux of the matter – to whom does art belong? – it's at its most compelling.
It is a competent biography of a complex and interesting character, but it lacks a bit of zest and never quite hits the right note.
I feel there is real potential here, but it is disappointing that it left so little of a mark on me.
The reality of Holy Fool is that this is a boring play, both dramatically and conceptually.
Other than this, the evening is neither offensive nor intriguing, but largely forgettable, a shame given what it might have been.
This is the lightly fictionalised story of the agonies faced by the composer Dimitri Shostakovich as he struggled to retain artistic freedom in Stalin’s Soviet Union.
It is a well-researched and finely crafted script, penned by Rosalind Adler and Lea Sellers, which never feels too bloated despite the almost forty-year span of the piece.
Whilst some scenes are a little drawn out, this is an interesting look at one man's struggle to continue making music, and stay alive, in turbulent times.
There is much to admire here: a strong ensemble and a story that places artistic freedom, morality and survival under uncomfortable scrutiny.
For a story about one of the twentieth century's greatest composers, this feels like a missed opportunity.
Still, the performances are beautifully judged, Kate Fahy's direction is clear, and the lighting and projections are used effectively.
Eventually, Holy Fool is nothing but a superficial, unenticing, and painfully boring piece, whose only appeal is the name it intends to honour — and fails to do so miserably.
Bending from a political thriller into a last-minute story of friendship, and not quite going into enough detail to be passable as a biographical piece, Holy Fool lacks a clear structure or climax.

Underground resistance and the human spirit is the story told here in an extremely well created and performed piece of work, with strong character acting and wry, comic moments to leaven the harsh story.
For a play about one of the 20th century’s most significant composers, that feels like a considerable omission.

cn.t: Mixed reviews for this Shostakovich drama: critics praise the timely subject matter and strong performances, but fault the sprawling, unfocused narrative and lack of musical integration. Some find it gripping; others call it sluggish and overlong.
